file_name: 2025 - An Extensive Investigation of Strategies in Baseball - William et al.md
universal_lens: A stochastic, zero-sum, perfect-information extensive-form game models baseball manager decisions as sequential choice nodes under probabilistic transitions and terminal utilities. A Bayesian game-theoretic framework for baseball decision-making integrates stochastic state transitions, infinite horizon dynamics, and strategic equilibrium computation under bounded rationality constraints.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference framework applied to manager decision states using conformal predictive distributions over action outcomes and win probabilities. GSI employs conformal predictive inference to map matchup models into probabilistic win probability estimates, enabling real-time Bayesian updating of team performance metrics across dynamic game states.
gse_mapping: Situation-aware state-transition engine encodes strategic choices via game tree traversal, updating belief states through observed actions and probabilistic outcomes. GSE utilizes structured state-transition graphs derived from baserunner-out configurations to simulate tactical decisions, leveraging minimal sufficient statistics for efficient expectiminimax search within truncated game trees.

primitives.breakdown_regime: When terminal states are reached, utility is determined by win/loss outcome; otherwise, transitions depend on probabilistic outcomes or strategic choices.

reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces foundational elements for constructing an AI manager capable of solving for a Subgame Perfect Equilibrium (SPE) in an extensive-form baseball game. The core challenge lies in the infinite nature of the state space, which arises because there is always a non-zero probability of scoring any number of runs in an inning or continuing play into extra innings indefinitely. To address this, the authors impose three key assumptions: (1) a team wins upon achieving a large run lead in an inning, (2) all extra innings are treated equivalently to the tenth, and (3) the resulting constrained state space remains finite yet significantly larger than simpler games such as Heads-Up Limit Hold’em. These constraints allow for tractable computation while preserving essential strategic complexity. The methodology hinges on defining a manageable subset of the game tree—specifically, a subtree rooted at the current decision point and ending at the conclusion of the next plate appearance. Within this subtree, win probabilities are estimated using a function Ω derived from historical data, enabling expectiminimax search to compute optimal strategies. This approach contrasts with naive Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), which performs poorly under these conditions. The paper emphasizes that real-world application demands rapid decision-making, necessitating efficient approximations rather than exhaustive searches. Thus, the framework bridges theoretical game theory with practical implementation by integrating empirical data-driven models into a structured decision-making architecture.
